'I had near-death experience - dying doesn't scare me after terror and ecstasy of what I saw'

Neuroscientist Dr Christof Koch has made a close study of near-death experiences after coming close to death himself during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic

12:09, 19 Sep 2026Updated 12:10, 19 Sep 2026

Stories of near-death experiences date back for many centuries. The first known example was recorded by Plato over 2,000 years ago, when a soldier from what is now southern Turkey told of his journey through the underworld after having been declared dead in battle.

‌

But in recent years the phenomenon has been come under increasing scrutiny by scientists. One researcher who has a particular insight on near-death experiences is neuroscientist Dr Christof Koch. He has made a close study of what he calls “power outages” in the brain, driven at least in part by his own experience when he suffered what he calls “a medical emergency” during the opening days of the Covid-19 pandemic.

‌

He described the "utterly remarkable” experience to The Times, explaining: "I saw overwhelming brightness and felt terror and ecstasy.

‌

”Nothing else no body, no self, no identity whatsoever. But also no world and no passage of time. Nothing except for an icy blue light.”

Dr Koch, who is based at the Allen Institute in Seattle says that the experience has completely changed his attitude to death. Like a lot of people who have experienced this phenomenon, he no longer fears dying: "In people who have undergone a near-death experience this is not uncommon. It's a so-far unexplained benefit.”

‌

Writing about the near-death experience [NDE] phenomenon in Scientific American, Dr Koch says that roughly one in 10 patients who suffer a cardiac arrest and are then revived reports experiencing a NDE: “Thousands of survivors of these harrowing touch-and-go situations tell of leaving their damaged bodies behind and encountering a realm beyond everyday existence, unconstrained by the usual boundaries of space and time.

“These powerful, mystical experiences can lead to permanent transformation of their lives.”

He says that many NDE experiencers report having met with deceased relatives, or spiritual beings such as angels. He describes how many people who have been through a near-death experience will see their life “flash before their eyes..”

‌

Some of these reports can be explained by simple physiological changes, he says. For example the “tunnel vision” described by people that have come close to death could be caused by reduced blood flow to the eyes.

However, some other aspects of the phenomenon defy easy scientific explanation. In 2006, French anaesthesiologist and researcher Dr. Jean-Jacques Charbonier presented a thought-provoking case at the First International Conference on Near-Death Experiences.

While undergoing major surgery, a female patient went into cardiac arrest and had a near-death experience. After being revived, she recalled how she felt as if she had floated up to the ceiling of the operating room.

Hovering near the ceiling of the operating theatre, she could see over a partition wall into the next room. There, she said, she could see as doctors amputated another patient's leg and placed the severed limb into a yellow clinical waste bag.

Later investigation, Dr Charbonier said, revealed that the woman’s observations were absolutely correct: “People who were brain-dead could see what was going on in a waiting room, or around them, in precise detail. We are not talking about an hallucination here because it was quite real,” he said.
